clue.text: Little sign of sun and forecast's not hot — you may need these

indicators.note: only a small token of the word sun is wanted, its opening letter
not says the following abbreviation is dropped from the forecast word

parts.note: a forecast reports the weather, so forecast's gives WEATHERS (weather's)
H is the usual abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A weather report promising little sunshine and no heat suggests you should wrap up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes H from WEATHERS, leaving WEATERS, after the S from 'Little sign of' sun. The definition is a cryptic pointer that only works once the surface's cold weather is pictured.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitted pullovers are what a chilly, sunless day calls for, so they are things you may need.

clue.text: Wrestler-in-chief wielded weapon

indicators.note: wielded suggests the letters are swung about and handled into a new order

explanation.surface: The top wrestler brandished a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wielded' rearranges all fifteen letters of 'Wrestler-in-chief'; the hyphens are ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A Winchester is a famous American repeating gun, a classic firearm of the Old West.

clue.text: Warning about British taking a part of Canada

indicators.note: about says the warning word goes round the abbreviation for British

parts.note: an alert is a warning

explanation.surface: A caution concerning Britain's involvement in a Canadian region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts B inside ALERT to make ALBERT, and 'taking' then adds A.
explanation.definitionFit: Alberta is one of Canada's western provinces, so it is a region of that country.

clue.text: Funds former wife's country house no end

parts.note: an ex is a former wife; the possessive adds no letter

indicators.note: no end says the final letter of the country house is dropped

parts.note: Chequers is the British Prime Minister's official country house in Buckinghamshire

explanation.surface: Money matters arising from an ex-wife's claim on a country estate.
explanation.walkthrough: CHEQUERS is the Prime Minister's country residence; 'no end' cuts its final S. The surface's divorce settlement hides the national treasury.
explanation.definitionFit: The Exchequer is the British government's treasury, the department holding the nation's money.

clue.text: Little woman's not mad about a Californian location

indicators.note: about says the sane word wraps round the little woman's name

parts.note: someone not mad is sane
Jo is one of the sisters in Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women; with the 's she gives JOS

explanation.surface: A small woman is no longer angry about a spot in California.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' is not a small lady but Jo March of Alcott's Little Women; JO'S goes inside SANE after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: San Jose is a large city in California's Silicon Valley, so it is a place in that state.

clue.text: Gangster: fellow in shady place

parts.note: Al Capone is the archetypal gangster, giving AL
cove is old British slang for a fellow or chap

explanation.surface: A mobster and his associate lurk in the shadows.
explanation.walkthrough: COVE is dated British slang for a man; AL is Capone, the crossword's stock gangster.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess set back into a wall or garden is sheltered from light, a shaded nook.

clue.text: Woman found instruction from proof reader beneath article

indicators.note: in a down entry beneath puts the proof reader's mark below the article

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
dele is the proofreading mark meaning delete

explanation.surface: A woman is discovered under a proof reader's marking on a newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: DELE (Latin 'delete') is the proofreader's instruction to cut text; 'beneath' places it under A in this down answer. The singer's name makes 'Woman' fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Adele is a female forename, borne by the famous English singer.

clue.text: Queen's entrance?

parts.note: a queen is also a female cat, so her way in is the little swinging door fitted in a house door

explanation.surface: How does Her Majesty come in?
explanation.walkthrough: The royal picture misleads: a queen is a female cat, and her 'entrance' is a small hinged pet door.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hinged flap in a door lets a pet come and go, so it is a feline's doorway.

clue.text: Fiddle scores

parts.note: fiddle is another word for the bowed string instrument, and scores are written musical works composed for it with orchestra

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' suggests cheating and 'scores' tallies, as if someone rigged results; in fact it is the instrument and its written music.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestral works featuring a solo fiddler are pieces of written music for that instrument.

clue.text: Lump results from first of knocks on head

indicators.note: first of picks out only the opening letter of knocks

parts.note: nob is slang for the head

explanation.surface: Being hit on the head leaves a bump.
explanation.walkthrough: NOB is old slang for the head; K, the opening letter of 'knocks', sits on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded protuberance or swelling is a lump.

clue.text: Car toll scam: terrible aggro in Chester mostly ensures

parts.note: a con is a scam or swindle

indicators.note: terrible says the letters that follow are thrown into disorder

parts.note: aggro is British slang for aggressive trouble, used here just for its letters

indicators.note: mostly means the city name loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A complaint that the road charge is a swindle causing ugly trouble in the city of Chester.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims Chester to CHESTE; 'terrible' then rearranges AGGRO + IN + CHESTE into GESTION CHARGE after CON. A congestion charge is a fee for driving into a busy city centre, as in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A fee levied on motorists entering a crowded city zone is a toll on cars.

clue.text: See 10
Covered live radio broadcast I missed

indicators.note: broadcast suggests the letters of the phrase are scattered about and reset
missed tells us one letter of the fodder is left out of the result

parts.note: taken as its letters for the rearrangement

explanation.surface: A live radio programme went out without me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges LIVE RADIO, and 'I missed' says the I is removed, leaving the letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laid over with a layer, such as gold leaf, has been covered.

clue.text: Country restricting trade union law

indicators.note: restricting says the country word hems in the union abbreviation

parts.note: a state is a country

explanation.surface: A nation clamps down on organised labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restricting' puts TU inside STATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A statute is a written act passed by a legislature, a formal piece of legislation.

clue.text: Paint section of grand epic tableau

indicators.note: section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A painter works on part of a vast heroic scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'grand' through 'epic' into 'tableau'.
explanation.definitionFit: To paint something is to represent or portray it in a picture.

clue.text: Speaking part in send-up has singular comic quality

indicators.note: in says the spoken part goes inside the turned word
up, in a down entry, means the word send is read from bottom to top
speaking says we want a word that sounds like the theatrical part

parts.note: a role is an acting part
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: An actor's line in a spoof has a uniquely funny character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaking' turns ROLE into the sound-alike ROLL, which goes 'in' DNES (SEND turned 'up'), then S follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Drollness is dry, whimsical humour, the trait of being amusingly odd.

clue.text: One requesting something to eat in pub

indicators.note: in places the food item inside the pub word

parts.note: a bar is a pub
an egg is a thing to eat

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a bite in the local.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts EGG inside BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant who asks passers-by for money or food is one who makes requests.

clue.text: Plimsoll — my gosh! — falls apart at end of race

indicators.note: falls apart says the exclamation breaks up and its letters are reassembled
at end of picks the final letter of race

explanation.surface: Goodness, a canvas trainer disintegrates as the runner finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: A plimsoll is a British name for a canvas sports shoe; 'falls apart' rearranges MY GOSH and the last letter of 'race' ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plimsoll is a light rubber-soled canvas sports shoe worn for physical education.

clue.text: Nameless crony meets mafia boss in outer London borough

indicators.note: nameless says the abbreviation for name is taken away from the pal word

parts.note: a don is a Mafia chief

explanation.surface: An unnamed friend meets a Mafia chief in a London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the abbreviation for name, removed from CRONY to leave CROY. CROYDON is a borough in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Croydon is a large borough on the southern edge of Greater London.

clue.text: Drink freely as musical's almost finished

indicators.note: almost finished says the show's name stops one letter short

parts.note: Carousel is the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical; the 's is just a link

explanation.surface: Theatregoers start drinking heavily as the show is nearly over.
explanation.walkthrough: Carousel is a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical; 'almost finished' cuts its last letter, L.
explanation.definitionFit: To carouse is to drink plentifully and make merry.

clue.text: The lady's terribly pale, perhaps

indicators.note: terribly says the letters of the phrase are scrambled badly into a new order

parts.note: the letters of 'the lady'; the possessive 's adds nothing

explanation.surface: A woman looks dreadfully washed-out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' looks like an adverb for 'pale' but rearranges THE LADY. 'perhaps' marks pale as one example of looking like death.
explanation.definitionFit: Deathly means resembling death, of which a ghastly pallor is one instance.

clue.text: One making pledge on behalf of someone close

parts.note: pro means in favour of, or for, someone
close can mean stingy, so a close person is a miser

explanation.surface: A guarantor acts on behalf of a nearby friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close' means tight-fisted, not near: a close person is a MISER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who vows or gives their word is one who pledges.

clue.text: School medical officer observed dunce

explanation.surface: The school doctor spotted a slow pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: SCHMO is American slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A schmo is American slang for a stupid or contemptible person.

clue.text: Parliamentarian cunningly fooled E Heath with ruse

indicators.note: cunningly suggests the letters are craftily rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An MP craftily deceived the former Prime Minister Edward Heath with a trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cunningly' rearranges FOOLED, E, HEATH and RUSE; 'with' only joins. Edward Heath was a British Conservative Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leader of the House of Commons is a senior MP who organises government business in Parliament.

clue.text: See 21
Feeling that enmity embodies

indicators.note: embodies says the phrase holds the answer within it

explanation.surface: Hostility contains an emotion.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle 'that' and 'enmity'; aptly, enmity is a kind of loathing.
explanation.definitionFit: Hate is an intense emotion of loathing.

clue.text: Cleric reaches final stage of pilgrimage to Italian region

parts.note: Ven is the abbreviation for Venerable, the title of an archdeacon

indicators.note: final stage of picks the last letter of pilgrimage

explanation.surface: A clergyman completes the last leg of his pilgrimage to Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: VEN abbreviates Venerable, an archdeacon's title. The Veneto is the region around Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: The Veneto is a region of north-east Italy whose capital is Venice.

clue.text: Bacon, for instance, is smothered in pesto after ends have been removed

indicators.note: smothered in says the pieces are buried inside the trimmed sauce
these words say the sauce loses its first and last letters

parts.note: say means for instance

explanation.surface: Bacon, as an example, is buried in pesto once it has been trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's bacon is a breakfast food, but here it is Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan writer of Essays. PESTO with its ends 'removed' gives EST, which SAY + IS goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon wrote a celebrated collection of short prose pieces called Essays.
